title: Reverse Linked List II
description: Brute force to optimized: extracting values and rebuilding versus an in-place fixed-anchor move-to-front reversal of just the target sub-range.

blocks.text: Given the head of a singly linked list, and two integers left and right (with left <= right), reverse only the nodes from position left to position right (1-indexed), and return the head of the modified list.

blocks.caption: Repeatedly pull the node right after the fixed "curr" pointer to the front of the sub-range

blocks.text: Given a linked list and two positions left and right, reverse only the nodes between those two positions (inclusive), leaving every other node exactly where it was.

blocks.title: Analogy: Reversing Only One Section of a Line of People
blocks.text: Like having a line of people and being asked to reverse the order of just one contiguous SECTION of the line (say, positions 2 through 4), while everyone before and after that section stays exactly where they are. Repeatedly picking up the person right after a fixed "anchor" point and moving them to the very front of the section being reversed, one at a time, achieves the reversal of just that section without disturbing anyone outside it.

blocks.caption: The fixed prev pointer anchors the sub-range; each iteration moves one more node to the front of it

{"headers":["Step","Result","Why"],"rows":[["A sub-range of a single node has nothing to actually reverse","The list stays unchanged","Reversing a single-element range trivially produces the same range"],["Answer","[5]","The list is returned unchanged"]]}

blocks.text: Before reversing the whole list and then trying to patch the untouched portions back in afterward, notice that a fixed "anchor" pointer, combined with repeatedly moving one node at a time to the front of the target range, reverses just that range directly.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Walking to the node just BEFORE position left (call it prev) gives a fixed anchor point whose next pointer needs to end up pointing at the NEW first node of the reversed sub-range.

Observation 2: The node originally AT position left (call it curr) will end up as the LAST node of the reversed sub-range, so it can stay fixed in place while everything after it, up to position right, gets moved in front of it one at a time.

Observation 3: At each step, the node immediately after curr is detached and re-inserted immediately after prev (at the front of the currently-reversed portion), which is exactly the effect of moving it to the front.

Observation 4: Repeating this detach-and-reinsert step exactly (right - left) times completes the reversal of the entire sub-range, with prev.next always correctly pointing at the current front of the (growing) reversed portion.

Recognizing that curr can stay FIXED as the sub-range's tail, while nodes are individually detached and moved to the front, avoids needing to reverse the sub-range separately and then reconnect both boundaries afterward.

This is a variation of iterative reversal specifically adapted for a bounded sub-range: a fixed anchor (prev) and a fixed tail (curr), with nodes individually moved to the front of the range one at a time.
Extract every value into a plain array, reverse just the specified sub-range of the array, then rebuild an entirely new linked list from the modified values.

items: Walk through the list, collecting every value into an array.
Reverse only the sub-array corresponding to positions left through right, then build a brand new linked list from the modified array.

codes.python:
def reverse_between(head, left, right):
    values = []
    node = head
    while node:
        values.append(node.val)                                            # collect every value into a plain array
        node = node.next
    values[left - 1:right] = reversed(values[left - 1:right])              # reverse only the specified sub-range
    dummy = ListNode(0)
    cur = dummy
    for v in values:
        cur.next = ListNode(v)                                             # rebuild a brand new list from the modified values
        cur = cur.next
    return dummy.next


if __name__ == "__main__":
    head = ListNode(1, ListNode(2, ListNode(3, ListNode(4, ListNode(5)))))
    result = reverse_between(head, 2, 4)
    values = []
    while result:
        values.append(result.val)
        result = result.next
    print(values)

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Values are collected first, since reversing a specific sub-range is trivial with array slicing, but awkward directly on a singly linked list.
Only the sub-array from index (left-1) to (right-1) is reversed, using 0-indexed array positions corresponding to the 1-indexed problem positions.
A brand new linked list is built from the modified values, since this brute force does not reuse any of the original nodes.

blocks.text: The specified sub-range is correctly identified and reversed, so the resulting list is always accurate.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), one pass to collect values plus one pass to rebuild.
Space: O(n), for the intermediate array and the entirely new set of nodes created.
Limitation: extracting values and creating brand new nodes ignores that the EXISTING nodes can simply be re-linked in place, reversing just the specified sub-range directly with O(1) extra space.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: The brute force rebuilds an entirely new list. Instead, walk to the node just before position left (prev), then keep curr fixed at position left itself (which becomes the sub-range's tail). Repeatedly detach the node right after curr and re-insert it immediately after prev, effectively moving it to the front of the currently-reversed portion. Repeating this exactly (right - left) times reverses the entire sub-range in place.

Use a dummy head. Walk prev forward (left - 1) times to reach the node just before the sub-range. Set curr to prev.next. Repeat (right - left) times: detach curr.next (call it next), set curr.next to next.next, set next.next to prev.next, and set prev.next to next. Return dummy.next.
Keep prev and curr fixed as anchors, repeatedly moving the node right after curr to the front of the sub-range.
Dry run for head = [1,2,3,4,5], left = 2, right = 4

blocks.title: Final answer
blocks.text: After 2 iterations (right - left = 4 - 2 = 2), the list is [1,4,3,2,5], matching the expected result.

codes.python:
def reverse_between(head, left, right):
    dummy = ListNode(0, head)
    prev = dummy
    for _ in range(left - 1):
        prev = prev.next                                                   # walk to the node just before the sub-range begins

    curr = prev.next                                                       # curr stays fixed as the sub-range's (shrinking) tail
    for _ in range(right - left):
        next_node = curr.next
        curr.next = next_node.next                                        # detach the node right after curr
        next_node.next = prev.next                                        # insert it at the very front of the sub-range
        prev.next = next_node
    return dummy.next


if __name__ == "__main__":
    head = ListNode(1, ListNode(2, ListNode(3, ListNode(4, ListNode(5)))))
    result = reverse_between(head, 2, 4)
    values = []
    while result:
        values.append(result.val)
        result = result.next
    print(values)

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), a single pass to reach the sub-range plus a bounded number of steps to reverse it.
Space: O(1) extra, reusing the existing nodes.

curr, fixed at the original position-left node, correctly ends up as the LAST node of the reversed sub-range, since it never moves while every node originally after it gets pulled in front of it one at a time. prev.next always points to whatever is currently the FRONT of the (partially) reversed sub-range, so each new node inserted right after prev correctly becomes the new front. After exactly (right - left) iterations, every node from left+1 to right has been moved to the front in reverse order, completing the reversal, with prev and curr correctly bounding the untouched parts of the list on either side.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","What happens"],"rows":[["Each iteration","The node right after curr is detached and re-inserted immediately after prev, becoming the new front of the reversed portion"],["After (right - left) iterations","The entire sub-range from left to right has been reversed in place"]]}

items: The dummy head lets prev correctly walk to "the node before position left" even when left is 1 (meaning the reversal starts at the true head).
curr never moves during the reversal loop, correctly ending up as the tail of the reversed sub-range.
The three-line detach-and-reinsert sequence (curr.next = next.next; next.next = prev.next; prev.next = next) must happen in exactly this order to avoid losing track of any pointer.

blocks.text: Reversing only a bounded sub-range of a linked list can be done in place by keeping a fixed anchor just before the range and a fixed tail at the range's original start, repeatedly moving each subsequent node to the front of the range.

items: Getting the three-line pointer reassignment out of order, which can lose track of part of the list entirely.
Off-by-one errors in the number of iterations (right - left) or in walking prev to the correct starting position (left - 1 steps).
Forgetting the dummy head, which would require awkward special-case logic when left = 1 (reversing starting from the true head).

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: "Reverse only a SUB-RANGE of a linked list" points toward a fixed anchor pointer just before the range, combined with repeatedly moving each subsequent node to the front of the range, rather than reversing the whole list.

items: How would you extend this to reverse the list in groups of k, repeated across the WHOLE list? This becomes Reverse Nodes in k-Group, applying this same sub-range reversal technique repeatedly, once per group.

How would you verify your solution handles left = 1 correctly? Trace through an example where the dummy head's role (letting prev "exist" before the true head) is essential, confirming no special-casing is needed.
What if the list were doubly linked instead? The same core technique still applies, though each node's "previous" pointer would also need updating to remain consistent throughout the reversal.
A bounded-range variation of Reverse Linked List's core reversal technique, directly extended (and applied repeatedly) in Reverse Nodes in k-Group elsewhere in this category.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text:
Brute force: O(n) time, O(n) space.
Optimized (fixed anchor, move-to-front reversal): O(n) time, O(1) space.

items: Pattern: Fixed anchor (prev) and fixed tail (curr), repeatedly moving each subsequent node to the front of the sub-range
Core Idea: curr stays fixed as the sub-range's eventual tail; each iteration detaches the next node and re-inserts it right after the fixed anchor
Time: O(n)
Space: O(1)
Most Important Observation: The node originally at position left never moves; it becomes the reversed sub-range's tail while everything after it is moved to the front one at a time
Interview Difficulty: Medium
One-line memory trick: next=curr.next; curr.next=next.next; next.next=prev.next; prev.next=next, repeated (right-left) times
